text: Open your fridge tonight and look inside.
Milk from last week. Yesterday's rice. A tomato that's still red.
Without that cold box, most of it would start rotting within a day or two.
Now imagine a world with no fridge, no freezer, no packet and no can.
Rewind ten thousand years.
A hunter brings home a whole deer.
That's far more meat than one family can eat before it spoils.
And spoiled food wasn't just wasteful. It could kill you.
The enemy was invisible. Bacteria and mould, feeding on the same food you needed.
So people learned to fight back.
The first weapon was the sun.
Strips of meat, fish and fruit were laid out to dry, because microbes need water to grow.
The second weapon was fire.
Hung above the hearth, meat dried even faster, and the smoke coated it in chemicals that bacteria hate.
Then came salt.
Salt pulls water out of food. Pack fish or meat in it, and it can last for months.
And here's the strange part.
One of the best tricks used microbes to beat microbes.
In southern Sweden, archaeologists found a pit where people fermented fish about nine thousand two hundred years ago.
Fermenting lets friendly microbes take over, and they make the food so sour that dangerous ones can't survive.
It's the same idea behind yoghurt, pickles and idli batter today.
But what about keeping things cold in the desert?
Around two thousand four hundred years ago, Persians built huge mud-brick domes called yakhchals.
In winter they filled them with ice, and some kept it frozen right through the summer.
Then, an army changed everything.
France's soldiers needed food that could survive long marches.
So the government offered a prize, and a Paris cook named Nicolas Appert won it, by sealing cooked food in glass jars and boiling them.
In eighteen ten, an Englishman named Peter Durand patented the same idea using tin cans.
Sun. Smoke. Salt. Fermenting. Ice. Sealed jars.
Every one of them does the same job. It stops tiny living things from eating your food first.
So tonight, when you open the fridge and the light comes on, remember.
You're looking at a ten-thousand-year-old war, finally won by a cold little box.
